• Capex: a benchmark-based estimate, presented as a range
• Opex, lifecycle, battery augmentation
• P50 and P90 yields; tariff partly indexed to USD
• Project IRR and NPV at the hurdle; proceed to bid
scenes.visual: Layout: A feasibility dashboard assembling: capex range bar. 0-2s: fade in. 2-21s: a capex range bar appears labelled 'benchmark estimate: range, not a point'. 21-33s: a yield distribution shows P50 and P90 markers. 33-47s: an appraisal card shows NPV positive and IRR above hurdle. 47-61s: a 'proceed to bid: development budget at risk' stamp lands. 61-63s: hold, then cut.

scenes.narration: Stage two, structuring. The SPV is formed with a developer holding sixty per cent and a strategic partner forty. The contracts: an EPC turnkey contract with a fixed price, a fixed date and liquidated damages; an O and M agreement; the PPA; a land lease; a grid connection agreement; and direct agreements for lenders. The team completes a risk allocation matrix and finds exactly the gap we've discussed several times: EPC delay damages didn't cover the PPA's late-COD penalties plus debt service during a delay. They fix it with higher delay damage rates and sponsor completion support. An environmental and social assessment is carried out to lenders' standards. The question here: if construction ran six months late, who would pay for each day, and is anything left with the SPV that it can't bear?
scenes.onScreen:
Stage 2: structuring and bankability
• SPV: developer 60%, strategic partner 40%
• EPC turnkey, O&M, PPA, land, grid, direct agreements
• Gap: EPC delay LDs versus PPA late-COD penalties
• Fixed with higher LD rates and completion support
scenes.visual: Layout: The SPV contract hub building, with one gap flashing between EPC and PPA, then closing. 0-2s: fade in. 2-15s: an SPV hub forms with two sponsor stakes, 60 and 40. 15-32s: contract spokes draw: EPC, O&M, PPA, land, grid, direct agreements. 32-41s: a gap flashes red between EPC and PPA. 41-56s: a patch 'higher LD rates + completion support' closes the gap. 56-58s: hold, then cut.

scenes.narration: Stage three, modelling. The model follows the principles you've learned: separate inputs, a timing sheet with flags, clean calculation blocks, outputs, and a checks sheet with a master check. CFADS is built on P90 for the lenders' case and P50 for the equity case. Debt is sized at the lower of DSCR sculpting, with a target set by lenders for contracted solar, and a gearing cap. The illustrative result: debt of one hundred and thirty-five million, seventy-five per cent, equity of forty-five million, and the DSRA funded at close with a letter of credit. In the base case DSCR is flat at target, LLCR at the start roughly equals the target, and PLCR is higher thanks to a PPA tail beyond debt maturity. Sensitivities cover delay, capex and opex overruns, a P99 yield and a combined downside: debt service is covered in every case, but equity returns are thin in the combined downside. The question: why size on P90 but evaluate equity on P50?
scenes.onScreen:

• Structured model: inputs, flags, checks, master check
• P90 CFADS for lenders; P50 for equity
• Debt 135M (75%) by the lower of sculpting and gearing cap
• Sensitivities: debt covered in all; equity thin in combined downside

scenes.narration: Stage four, diligence and close. Technical, legal, insurance, model audit, tax and environmental and social reports all feed the lenders' base case. The CP checklist is tracked weekly, and the longest-lead item turns out to be an amendment to the grid connection agreement, exactly the kind of third-party dependency that slips closes. Interest rate swaps are executed at close, and the tariff is adjusted according to the bid rules for swap movements. Financial close is achieved, and the first drawdown follows the agreed order: equity first, then pro rata with debt. The question: what would happen to debt capacity if interest rates had risen by one per cent before the swaps were executed? And which CPs would you have escalated six months earlier?

scenes.narration: Stage five, construction. Monthly drawdowns come with independent engineer certification and funding sufficiency tests. Estimate at completion is tracked by cost category. Contingency is drawn down for a transformer delay, and the claims log is monitored. AI is used to extract obligations from the contracts into a compliance tracker and to draft monthly lender reports, all reviewed and signed by the finance lead. Commercial operation arrives two weeks late, and the delay damages cover lost revenue and debt service, just as the stage two fix intended. Stage six, operations. Quarterly reports cover availability, output against P50 and P90, opex, DSCR and reserves. In year three, low irradiance and an inverter fault push DSCR close to lock-up. The team explains the variance by volume and availability, increases spares holdings, and talks to lenders early. By year five, a refinancing opportunity arises, with any gains shared according to the contract's provisions.

scenes.narration: Let me work through the capstone questions the way I'd want you to answer them in an interview or an exam. Why size debt on P90 but evaluate equity on P50? Because lenders need confidence in debt service under downside conditions, while equity accepts more risk in return for higher expected returns. What if interest rates rose one per cent before hedging? Debt capacity falls, because the same maximum debt service has a lower present value at a higher rate. Which contracts protect CFADS in a long construction delay? EPC delay damages, sponsor completion support, delay-in-start-up insurance if purchased, and the PPA's own provisions. How would a lock-up affect sponsors? Distributions are deferred and cash trapped, lowering equity IRR even if the cash is later released. And which AI uses needed the highest tier? Figures in lender reports, compliance certificates and any model change affecting the base case.

scenes.narration: The mistakes that recur across deals: optimistic early estimates becoming fixed budgets, gaps between contracts discovered late, models that are hard to audit, CP tracking left to the last month, and reporting that surprises lenders rather than informing them early. So, to recap the whole journey. Feasibility sets honest ranges. Structuring allocates risk so contracts fit together. Modelling turns contracts into CFADS and debt capacity, tested with sensitivities. Diligence and close convert agreement into funding. Construction protects the budget with controls and evidence. And operations keep lenders informed with early, honest reporting. Your try-this-now: write your own one-page capstone for a different asset type, perhaps a toll road or a hospital PPP, covering all six stages and the key question a deal team should ask at each.

pool.question: A utility wants to build a plant without exposing its other businesses if the plant fails. Which approach best achieves this?
options: Corporate loan guaranteed by the parent
Project finance through a ring-fenced SPV
pool.explanation: Project finance isolates the plant in an SPV with lenders looking mainly to its cash flows; the other options put the parent's balance sheet at risk.

pool.question: Which of these is a 'use' of funds in a project finance sources and uses table?
pool.explanation: Interest during construction must be funded, so it is a use. Debt, equity and grants are sources.

pool.question: Cash flows: −2,000 today, then 800 per year for 3 years. At 10%, what is the NPV (annuity factor 2.4869)?
pool.explanation: PV of inflows = 800 × 2.4869 ≈ 1,989.5; NPV ≈ 1,989.5 − 2,000 ≈ −10.5. The project slightly fails to earn 10%.

pool.question: Project P has NPV 250 and IRR 14%; Project Q has NPV 180 and IRR 22%. They are mutually exclusive and evaluated at the same cost of capital. Which should be chosen?
options: P, because it adds more value
pool.explanation: With mutually exclusive projects, higher NPV adds more value. IRR ignores scale and reinvestment assumptions.

pool.question: An analyst discounts nominal cash flows (including 6% inflation) using a real discount rate. What is the likely effect?
options: NPV is overstated because future inflated cash flows are discounted too lightly
No effect, because inflation cancels out
pool.explanation: Mixing nominal cash flows with a real rate under-discounts future amounts, inflating NPV. Consistency is required.

pool.question: Which statements about payback are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: A shorter payback always means a higher NPV
Payback ignores cash flows after the payback point
Discounted payback is longer than simple payback for a conventional project with positive discount rate
Simple payback ignores the time value of money
pool.explanation: Payback has known limitations; a shorter payback does not guarantee higher NPV because later cash flows are ignored.

pool.question: Which cost is typically capex?
options: Construction of a new pumping station
pool.explanation: Building a long-lived asset is capital expenditure; the others are operating costs.

pool.question: Which funding source is repaid first in the capital stack?
pool.explanation: Senior debt has priority in the waterfall and on security; equity is last.

pool.question: Debt 70% at 9% pre-tax, tax rate 20%, equity 30% at 16%. What is the WACC?
Which features make an offtake contract more bankable? (Select all that apply.)
options: Clear tariff and termination payment provisions
Offtaker may terminate for convenience without compensation
Tenor at least as long as the debt, ideally with a tail
pool.explanation: Creditworthiness, adequate tenor and clear payment and termination terms support debt repayment. Termination without compensation undermines bankability.

pool.question: An EPC contract caps delay liquidated damages at 5% of the contract price, but a six-month delay would cost the SPV roughly 12% of the contract price in lost revenue and debt service. What is the best response?
options: Raise the cap or add sponsor completion support or delay insurance to close the gap
Accept it because an EPC contract always transfers delay risk
pool.explanation: A low cap makes the risk transfer partial; lenders will require the gap to be covered by other mechanisms.

pool.question: When comparing tender bids, what should happen to a low bid with significant exclusions?
options: Price the exclusions to normalise it before comparison
pool.explanation: Normalisation reveals the true comparable cost; unpriced exclusions become owner costs later.

pool.question: Revenue is in local currency, while 70% of debt is in USD. What is the main risk and a typical mitigation?
options: Interest rate risk; issue more equity
Currency mismatch; use tariff indexation to USD, local-currency debt or hedging
pool.explanation: Depreciation of the local currency would raise debt service in local terms. Indexation, local debt or hedges address this.

pool.question: A project returns 8% on total capital; debt costs 7%. What happens to equity returns as gearing increases from 50% to 85% (ignoring tax)?
options: They fall because debt is expensive
They rise to 15% with no change in risk
They rise, from 9% to about 13.7%, but equity becomes much more sensitive to cash flow falls
pool.explanation: At 50%: (8 − 3.5)/50 = 9%. At 85%: (8 − 5.95)/15 ≈ 13.7%. Leverage magnifies both returns and risk.

pool.question: Where should hard-coded assumptions be placed in a well-structured model?
options: In clearly labelled input sheets with sources
pool.explanation: Separating inputs makes assumptions visible, changeable and auditable.

pool.question: Which are standard integrity checks in a project finance model? (Select all that apply.)
options: Cash balance never negative unless intended
Sources equal uses at the end of construction
pool.explanation: Integrity checks test the model's mechanics; an IRR level is an outcome, not a check.

pool.question: A 50 MW plant has a 22% capacity factor and 98% availability. What is its approximate annual output?
A model's revenue formula changes partway across the timeline from indexed to unindexed without a flag or note. What is the best fix?
options: Leave it, since the result may be intentional
Use a single consistent formula with a flag or input controlling indexation periods
pool.explanation: One formula per row with flags keeps logic transparent and auditable; hidden changes are a common source of errors.

pool.question: What is the purpose of a scenario selector?
options: To switch between stored input sets without overwriting the base case
pool.explanation: Selectors keep cases reproducible and protect the base case.

pool.question: Lenders' sensitivity results show minimum DSCR of 1.04x in the combined downside while all single sensitivities are above 1.15x. What does this suggest?
options: Debt service is covered but with a thin margin when risks coincide; lenders may seek extra protection
pool.explanation: Combined cases test coinciding risks. A thin margin may lead to reserves, sweeps or lower gearing, not automatic rejection.

pool.question: Why can financing fees and DSRA funding create circularity in a project finance model?
options: They depend on debt size, which depends on total uses that include them
pool.explanation: Debt funds uses; if uses include debt-dependent items, the calculation loops and must be solved deliberately.

pool.question: CFADS is 24 and debt service is 20. What is the DSCR?
pool.explanation: DSCR = CFADS / debt service = 24 / 20 = 1.20x.

pool.question: CFADS is 12M per year for 5 years; target DSCR 1.25x; rate 6% (annuity factor 4.2124). What is the DSCR-sized debt?
pool.explanation: Max debt service = 12/1.25 = 9.6M; debt = 9.6 × 4.2124 ≈ 40.4M.

pool.question: Which ratio uses the NPV of CFADS over the remaining loan life divided by debt outstanding?
pool.explanation: LLCR is the forward-looking loan-life ratio. PLCR uses the whole project life.

pool.question: Historic DSCR is 1.08x; lock-up is 1.15x and default is 1.05x. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Sponsors should engage lenders early with projections and actions
Lenders can immediately accelerate the loan
No event of default has occurred on this test
pool.explanation: The ratio is below lock-up but above default. Acceleration requires an event of default.

pool.question: What is typically the first item paid from revenue in the operating waterfall?
pool.explanation: Opex and taxes keep the project running and are paid before debt service and equity.

pool.question: Why does sculpting increase debt capacity compared with equal annuity repayments when CFADS varies?
options: Debt service follows CFADS so no single weak year constrains the whole loan
pool.explanation: With an annuity, the lowest-CFADS year limits debt; sculpting sets each period's debt service to CFADS ÷ target DSCR.

pool.question: NPV of CFADS over remaining loan life is 90M, over remaining project life is 126M; debt outstanding is 72M. What are LLCR and PLCR?
pool.explanation: LLCR = 90/72 = 1.25x; PLCR = 126/72 = 1.75x. PLCR is higher because it includes the tail.

pool.question: In a toll-road concession paid by users, who typically bears traffic (demand) risk?
pool.explanation: User-pays concessions transfer demand risk to the private party, which is why debt is sized conservatively.

pool.question: A hospital PPP deducts payments when an operating theatre is unavailable. How does the SPV typically protect CFADS?
options: By passing deductions down to its facilities management subcontractor back-to-back
pool.explanation: Back-to-back pass-down to the party responsible protects the SPV and lenders.

pool.question: What defines financial close?
options: Finance documents signed and conditions precedent satisfied, allowing drawdown
pool.explanation: Financial close is when funding becomes available; construction completion comes later.

pool.question: Which are typical conditions precedent to first drawdown? (Select all that apply.)
pool.explanation: CPs cover contracts, legal and security, insurance and permits. Operating accounts cannot exist before operations.

pool.question: Forecast cost to complete is 195; undrawn debt 150, remaining equity 40, remaining contingency 12. A pending contractor claim could add 15. What is the prudent conclusion?
options: The claim should be ignored until it is settled
Funding is sufficient today by 7, but the claim could create an 8 shortfall; plan mitigation now
Funding is sufficient by 22, so no action is needed
pool.explanation: Available = 150 + 40 + 12 = 202 versus 195 needed: headroom of 7. If the 15 claim materialises, cost rises to 210 and there is an 8 shortfall, so mitigation (settlement strategy, standby equity) should start now.

pool.question: What does a value-for-money assessment compare?
options: The EPC price with the O&M price
The PPA tariff with market prices only
The risk-adjusted whole-life cost of the PPP with conventional public delivery
pool.explanation: VfM tests whether the PPP delivers better value than a public sector comparator.

pool.question: Why are development costs described as 'at risk'?
options: They are always recovered through tariffs
They may not be recovered if the project fails to reach financial close
pool.explanation: Sponsors fund development before financing is secured; failure to close can mean losing them.

pool.question: Which is an appropriate AI use in project finance due diligence?
options: Extracting key contract terms with clause citations for lawyers to verify
pool.explanation: AI can accelerate extraction when humans verify; decisions and independent audits remain human responsibilities.

pool.question: An AI-drafted lender report quotes a DSCR of 1.34x; the locked model shows 1.31x. What should the reviewer do?
options: Correct it to the locked model output and investigate which input the AI used
Remove the DSCR from the report
pool.explanation: High-tier documents require reconciliation to locked outputs and a traceable fix to the workflow.

pool.question: Which practices improve the reliability of AI-assisted model review? (Select all that apply.)
options: Allowing AI to overwrite the base case directly
Testing AI-drafted formulas against hand calculations
Recording what the AI changed and who approved it
Asking for cell references for every finding
pool.explanation: Testing, citations and audit trails keep AI assistance verifiable. Direct overwrites of the base case bypass control.

pool.question: An analyst pastes confidential data-room documents into a public AI tool not approved by the firm to speed up review. What is the main issue?
options: The tool will produce wrong DSCRs
Breach of confidentiality obligations and firm AI policy
pool.explanation: Data rooms carry confidentiality obligations; only approved tools with appropriate protections may be used.

pool.question: Which element is part of model risk management?
options: Independent validation before models are used for decisions
Using AI outputs without review when deadlines are tight
pool.explanation: Validation, documentation and change control underpin model risk management.

pool.question: What is the right role of machine-learning output forecasts for an operating solar portfolio?
options: Documented inputs to discussion alongside independent, transparent methods
A reason to stop reporting to lenders
Automatic replacement of the lenders' base case
pool.explanation: ML forecasts can inform, but lender cases and decisions rely on transparent, validated methods and human judgment.

pool.question: A reviewer finds a row where the formula changes in one period to a typed value, several formulas containing 0.92 and 365, and no checks sheet. Which response best reflects widely used modelling conventions?
options: Leave the model as it is because the outputs look reasonable
Move constants to labelled inputs, restore consistent row formulas, add a checks sheet with a master check, and log the findings
Switch on iterative calculation to stabilise the results
Hide the affected rows before the lender audit
pool.explanation: Conventions such as FAST require labelled inputs, one formula per row and visible checks. Hiding or ignoring issues makes errors harder to find and would be flagged by any model audit.

pool.question: Before a formal lender model audit, a sponsor runs an internal review. Which activities belong in a structured review? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Reading the term sheet and key contracts to confirm the model reflects them
Automated scans for inconsistent row formulas and hard-codes
Reconciling the first operating year by hand
Deleting the checks sheet to simplify the file
Running the agreed sensitivities and confirming the master check stays at zero
pool.explanation: A review covers contract alignment, mechanical checks, reasonableness and scenario integrity. Removing checks reduces transparency.

pool.question: An analyst enters =NPV(10%, B2:F2) where B2 is the year-0 investment of -1,000 and gets 61.3. The hand calculation gives 67.4. What is wrong?
options: Excel NPV discounts the first value by one period; the correct formula is =B2+NPV(10%, C2:F2)
NPV cannot be used for project cash flows
The IRR function should be used instead
pool.explanation: Excel NPV assumes the first value falls at the end of period 1. Add the time-0 cash flow outside the function. Note that numpy-financial npv treats the first value as time 0.

pool.question: A Monte Carlo on CFADS for a loan sculpted at 1.30x on P50 cash flows shows about a 30% chance that at least one year falls below a 1.10x lock-up. What is the most useful conclusion for the deal team?
options: Monte Carlo results should be ignored in favour of the base case
Sizing on P50 leaves a material chance of lock-up; sizing on a conservative case such as P90, or adding structural protection, improves resilience
The target DSCR should be reduced to 1.10x
Lock-up tests should be removed from the loan agreement
pool.explanation: The simulation quantifies why lenders size on downside cases. Lowering the target or removing tests increases risk rather than managing it.

pool.question: A Python shadow model and the audited spreadsheet give different LLCRs. What is the role of the shadow model?
options: It replaces the audited model as the model of record
It is an independent check; differences are investigated against loan agreement definitions and resolved
It is used only for presentations
It should be discarded if it disagrees with the spreadsheet
pool.explanation: A shadow model verifies; the audited model remains the reference. Differences reveal either errors or definitional choices such as DSRA treatment.

pool.question: Six months before target close, a CP depends on a government land registry, and the realistic date is two weeks after target close. What should the deal team do?
options: Wait, because government CPs are always waived
Escalate now: engage the authority, plan bid bond and COD extensions, and consider a limited notice to proceed if needed
Remove the CP from the tracker
Ask lenders to sign without land rights
pool.explanation: Dependencies on public bodies are where closes slip. Early escalation and contingency planning are far cheaper than last-minute extensions.

pool.question: A team uses an approved AI tool to extract terms from a 400-page data room. Which practices make the output defensible? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Requiring a clause reference and verbatim quote for every extracted term
Having a qualified reviewer mark each item confirmed, corrected or unclear
Storing the AI draft, the verified matrix and the reviewer notes together
Treating terms the AI marked as certain as verified
Asking the tool to list what it could not determine
pool.explanation: Citations, human verification, a stored audit trail and explicit uncertainty make AI-assisted diligence defensible. AI confidence is not verification.
